lessons.title: What is trichology and why it matters
lessons.description: Understanding the science of hair and scalp health
lessons.content:
## Why Trichology Matters to You

If you're reading this, you already care about hair. But trichology takes that care to another level entirely. **Trichology is the scientific study of hair and scalp health** — the bridge between the salon chair and the clinic. It's the knowledge that transforms a good stylist into someone clients truly trust with their concerns.

In my thirty years of practice, I've seen thousands of clients who went to their hairdresser first — before their GP, before a dermatologist, before anyone. That tells you something profound about the relationship you already have with your clients. Trichology gives you the language and understanding to honour that trust.

> I always say to my students: your clients are already talking to you about their hair concerns. Trichology simply gives you the confidence to listen properly and respond wisely.

## The Landscape: Who Does What

Understanding boundaries is just as important as understanding science. Here's how the professionals fit together:

- **Hairstylists and barbers** — observe, advise on care, perform cosmetic treatments, and refer when needed
- **Trichologists** — assess hair and scalp conditions, provide non-medical treatment plans, and bridge the gap between salon and clinic
- **Dermatologists** — diagnose and treat medical skin and scalp conditions, prescribe medication
- **GPs** — investigate underlying health issues, run blood tests, manage systemic conditions

None of these roles exist in isolation. The best outcomes for clients happen when professionals communicate and collaborate. Throughout this course, you'll learn not just what you *can* do, but when to involve others — and how to do it gracefully.

## The Architecture of Hair and Scalp

Before you can understand what goes wrong, you need to understand what's meant to happen. Let's start with the scalp itself.

**The scalp has three layers:**

1. **Epidermis** — the outermost layer, your barrier against the world. It renews roughly every 28 days. When this cycle is disrupted, you see flaking, dryness, or excessive oiliness.
2. **Dermis** — the middle layer, packed with blood vessels, nerve endings, and the all-important **hair follicles**. This is where growth happens.
3. **Hypodermis** — the deepest layer, providing cushioning and insulation. It contains fat cells and the base of the largest follicles.

**Each hair strand has three components:**

- **Cuticle** — the protective outer layer, like tiles on a roof. When the cuticle is smooth and intact, hair shines. When it's damaged, hair feels rough, tangles easily, and breaks.
- **Cortex** — the bulk of the hair shaft, containing melanin (colour) and keratin bonds (strength). Chemical services like colouring and perming work in the cortex.
- **Medulla** — the innermost core, present in thicker hair. Its exact function is still debated, but it contributes to hair's overall structure.

**Sebaceous glands** sit alongside each follicle and produce **sebum**, the scalp's natural oil. Sebum protects the scalp barrier, keeps hair supple, and creates the microbiome environment that influences scalp health. Too much sebum contributes to greasy scalp and seborrhoeic conditions. Too little leads to dryness and irritation.

> Think of the scalp as a garden. The follicles are the plants, the dermis is the soil, and sebum is the rain. If any one element is out of balance, everything suffers. Your job is to learn how to read the garden.

## Why This Foundation Matters

Every treatment decision you make — every product you recommend, every service you offer, every referral you write — rests on understanding these basics. When a client asks why their hair is breaking, you'll know to look at the cuticle. When they mention an itchy scalp, you'll think about the epidermis and sebum balance. When they're losing hair, you'll consider the dermis and what's happening at the follicle level.

This isn't about becoming a doctor. It's about becoming the most knowledgeable, trustworthy version of yourself — the professional who can look at a scalp and understand what they're seeing.

## Key Takeaways

- Trichology bridges the gap between salon care and clinical treatment
- Understanding professional boundaries protects you and your clients
- The scalp has three layers (epidermis, dermis, hypodermis), each playing a distinct role in hair health
- Hair strands have three components (cuticle, cortex, medulla) that determine appearance and strength
- Sebaceous glands regulate scalp moisture and create the environment for healthy growth

## Reflection

Think about the last client who mentioned a hair or scalp concern to you. What did they say, and how did you respond? How might your response change now that you understand the basic architecture of hair and scalp?

lessons.title: Hair growth cycle and growth patterns
lessons.description: Anagen, catagen, telogen, exogen — and why it matters clinically
lessons.content:
## The Hair Growth Cycle

Every hair on your head is on its own individual journey. Understanding this journey is fundamental to everything you'll do in trichology — from explaining shedding to a worried client, to understanding why treatments take months to show results.

**The four phases of hair growth:**

### Anagen — The Growth Phase

This is where the magic happens. During **anagen**, the hair follicle is actively producing a new hair shaft. The cells in the **hair matrix** (at the base of the follicle) are dividing rapidly — in fact, they're among the fastest-dividing cells in the human body.

- Anagen lasts **2 to 7 years** on the scalp
- The length of anagen determines maximum hair length
- At any given time, approximately **85-90% of your scalp hair** is in anagen
- Genetics primarily determine anagen duration, which is why some people can grow waist-length hair and others plateau at shoulder length

### Catagen — The Transition Phase

When the follicle receives the signal to stop growing, it enters **catagen**. This is a brief transitional phase lasting about **2-3 weeks**. The lower portion of the follicle shrinks, and the hair detaches from its blood supply. The hair is now called a **club hair**.

### Telogen — The Resting Phase

During **telogen**, the follicle rests for approximately **3-4 months**. The club hair sits loosely in the follicle. About **10-15% of scalp hair** is in telogen at any time. This is the phase that becomes clinically significant in **telogen effluvium**, where a trigger pushes an abnormally high percentage of hairs into telogen simultaneously.

### Exogen — The Shedding Phase

The final release. The old club hair falls out — during brushing, washing, or simply through daily activity. **Normal shedding is 50-100 hairs per day**. This number is important: clients often think any shedding is abnormal, and you'll need to reassure them that shedding is a healthy sign of follicle cycling.

> When clients tell me they're losing hair, my first question is always: "How much?" Fifty to a hundred hairs a day sounds like a lot when you see them in the shower drain, but it's completely normal. Context is everything.

## Hair Across Ethnicities

Hair isn't one-size-fits-all, and understanding **ethnic variations** is critical for providing appropriate advice and avoiding damage.

- **Type 1 (Straight)** — typically associated with Asian and some European hair. Round follicle cross-section, high density, strong tensile strength. The cuticle layers are tightly packed, giving excellent shine but making chemical penetration slower.
- **Type 2 (Wavy)** — common in European hair. Slightly oval follicles. Varies from fine waves to more defined S-patterns.
- **Type 3 (Curly)** — oval to elliptical follicles. More prone to dryness because sebum travels more slowly down the spiral shaft.
- **Type 4 (Coily/Afro-textured)** — flat, elliptical follicles producing tight coils. **The most fragile hair type** — lower tensile strength, highest susceptibility to breakage, and often the driest because sebum barely travels past the first curl.

Each type requires different handling, different product approaches, and different awareness of potential damage. What works for straight European hair can devastate Afro-textured hair, and vice versa.

## How Damage Happens

Hair damage falls into three categories:

- **Chemical damage** — bleach, relaxers, permanent colour, and perms all disrupt the cortex structure. Repeated chemical processing leads to progressive weakening.
- **Physical damage** — heat tools above 180°C, tight braids and ponytails, rough brushing on wet hair, and excessive tension during styling.
- **Environmental damage** — UV radiation, chlorinated water, hard water mineral deposits, and pollution particles that settle on the scalp and shaft.

**Porosity and elasticity testing** helps you assess the current state of the hair:

- **Porosity** — how readily hair absorbs and retains moisture. High porosity (damaged cuticle) means hair absorbs quickly but loses moisture just as fast.
- **Elasticity** — how much a wet hair can stretch before breaking. Healthy hair stretches about 30% of its length. Hair that snaps immediately needs protein. Hair that stretches and doesn't spring back needs moisture.

## Key Takeaways

- Hair cycles through anagen (growth), catagen (transition), telogen (rest), and exogen (shedding)
- Normal shedding is 50-100 hairs per day — reassure clients about this
- Hair type varies significantly across ethnicities, affecting care recommendations
- Damage comes from chemical, physical, and environmental sources
- Porosity and elasticity tests give you actionable data about hair condition

## Reflection

Consider a client with Afro-textured hair who uses heat tools daily and has chemical relaxer treatments every 6-8 weeks. What types of damage might be occurring simultaneously, and how would you approach the conversation about hair health?

resources.title: Hair Growth Cycle Reference Card
resources.content:
## Hair Growth Phases

| Phase | Duration | % of Hair | What Happens |
|-------|----------|-----------|-------------|
| **Anagen** | 2-7 years | 85-90% | Active growth from matrix cells |
| **Catagen** | 2-3 weeks | ~1% | Follicle shrinks, hair detaches from blood supply |
| **Telogen** | 3-4 months | 10-15% | Follicle rests, club hair sits loosely |
| **Exogen** | Ongoing | — | Old hair sheds (50-100/day is normal) |

## Porosity & Elasticity Quick Test

**Porosity (Float Test):**
1. Place clean, product-free hair in water
2. Floats = low porosity (cuticle intact)
3. Sinks slowly = normal porosity
4. Sinks fast = high porosity (damaged cuticle)

**Elasticity (Stretch Test):**
1. Take a single wet hair strand
2. Gently stretch between fingers
3. Springs back = good elasticity (balanced)
4. Snaps = needs protein
5. Stretches without returning = needs moisture

lessons.title: Common scalp conditions and referral boundaries
lessons.description: Differentiating presentations and knowing when to refer
lessons.content:
## Reading the Scalp

Today we move from theory into clinical observation. By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to look at a scalp and recognise the most common conditions you'll encounter — and, critically, you'll know when something needs to go beyond your chair.

> The most important skill I teach isn't identification — it's knowing the limits of your identification. Getting comfortable with saying "I think this needs a closer look from a specialist" is one of the most professional things you can do.

## Inflammatory and Scaling Conditions

### Dandruff (Pityriasis Capitis)

The most common scalp condition you'll see. **Dandruff** presents as white or greyish flakes on the scalp and shoulders. It's non-contagious, generally not itchy (or mildly so), and responds well to zinc pyrithione or ketoconazole shampoos. Dandruff is essentially a mild form of seborrhoeic dermatitis.

### Seborrhoeic Dermatitis

More significant than simple dandruff. Look for **red, inflamed patches** with **greasy, yellowish scales**, particularly around the hairline, behind the ears, and at the crown. It's caused by an overgrowth of **Malassezia yeast** on the skin. Clients often describe it as itchy and embarrassing. It's chronic and relapsing — it can be managed but not cured.

### Psoriasis

Psoriasis presents as **thick, well-defined, red plaques** covered with **silvery-white scales**. On the scalp, it often appears at the hairline, behind the ears, and at the nape. Unlike seb derm, psoriasis plaques are typically dry, not greasy. It's hereditary and immune-mediated. Scalp psoriasis can extend beyond the hairline onto the forehead, which is a helpful diagnostic clue.

### Eczema (Atopic Dermatitis)

Scalp eczema presents as **dry, itchy, sometimes cracked skin**. It's often associated with a history of asthma, hay fever, or childhood eczema. Contact dermatitis — a reaction to hair products, dyes, or fragrances — is a common type you'll encounter in the salon.

### Pityriasis Amiantacea

Less common but distinctive: **thick, silvery-white scales** that bind to the hair shaft like a cast, sometimes described as looking like asbestos. It can occur alongside psoriasis, eczema, or seb derm. It needs professional assessment.

## Hair Loss Conditions

### Alopecia Areata

An **autoimmune condition** causing **smooth, round patches** of complete hair loss. The patches are typically well-defined with normal-looking skin. You may see **exclamation mark hairs** at the edges — short, broken hairs that taper at the base. This always needs referral.

### Traction Alopecia

Caused by **sustained tension on the hair** — tight ponytails, braids, extensions, weaves, or religious head coverings. You'll see thinning or loss along the **tension lines**, typically at the hairline, temples, or above the ears. **This is the one hair loss condition you can directly help prevent** through styling advice.

### Trichotillomania

A compulsive behaviour where clients **pull out their own hair**. The resulting loss is often irregular, with broken hairs of varying lengths. This is a psychological condition that needs sensitive handling and referral to mental health support.

## Infections

### Tinea Capitis

**Fungal infection** of the scalp — and one you must recognise because it's **contagious**. Look for patchy hair loss with broken hair shafts, scaling, and sometimes pustules. It's most common in children but can affect adults. **Do not treat this in the salon.** Refer immediately.

### Folliculitis

**Inflamed hair follicles** that look like small red bumps or pustules. Can be caused by bacteria, friction, or occlusion. Mild cases may resolve on their own, but persistent or spreading folliculitis needs medical attention.

## When to Refer

This is the most important section of today's lesson. **Refer when you see:**

- Any suspected infection (redness, pustules, spreading, pain)
- Open wounds, bleeding, or crusting
- Smooth patches of complete hair loss (alopecia areata)
- Rapidly progressing hair loss
- Scarring or shiny, smooth areas where follicles appear destroyed
- Any condition that isn't responding to over-the-counter treatment after 4 weeks

**Safe language:** Use observations, not diagnoses. "I've noticed some changes in this area" rather than "You have psoriasis." Frame referrals positively: "I think a specialist could give you a really clear picture of what's going on."

## Key Takeaways

- Learn to recognise the visual differences between dandruff, seb derm, psoriasis, and eczema
- Traction alopecia is preventable through styling changes — this is your direct area of impact
- Tinea capitis is contagious — recognise it and refer immediately
- Always use observational language, never diagnostic language
- Building referral relationships with GPs and dermatologists strengthens your professional practice

## Reflection

A regular client comes in and you notice red, scaly patches extending from their hairline onto their forehead, with thick silvery scales. They mention it's been getting worse over the past few months. What condition might this suggest, and how would you handle the conversation?

## Quick Visual Differentiation

| **Seb Derm** | Greasy, yellowish | Red, inflamed | Hairline, ears, crown | Yes |

| **Eczema** | Dry, cracked | Pink/red | Variable | Very |
| **Tinea Capitis** | Scaling + broken hairs | Variable | Patchy | Variable |

## Referral Decision Tree

1. **Is it infectious?** (Pustules, spreading, broken hairs with scale) → **Refer immediately**
2. **Is there complete hair loss in patches?** → **Refer** (possible alopecia areata)
3. **Is there scarring or follicle destruction?** → **Refer urgently**
4. **Is it not responding to OTC treatment after 4 weeks?** → **Refer**
5. **Is the client distressed?** → **Refer** (even if mild, distress warrants professional support)

lessons.title: Active ingredients and treatment techniques
lessons.description: From salicylic acid to LED therapy — what works and when
lessons.content:
## The Science Behind Scalp Treatments

Knowing that a scalp needs treatment is one thing. Knowing *which* treatment — and *why* — is what sets you apart. Today we move into the practical science of active ingredients and treatment modalities that you can confidently integrate into your practice.

## Key Active Ingredients

### Salicylic Acid

A **beta-hydroxy acid (BHA)** that works by breaking down the bonds between dead skin cells. It's **keratolytic** — it dissolves the protein that holds flakes together. Ideal for dandruff, mild psoriasis, and product build-up. Concentrations of 1-3% are typical in scalp products.

### Niacinamide (Vitamin B3)

An anti-inflammatory powerhouse. **Niacinamide** calms redness, supports the skin barrier, and helps regulate sebum production. It's gentle enough for sensitive scalps and works well alongside other active ingredients. Look for it in leave-on scalp serums.

### Caffeine

When applied topically, **caffeine** stimulates blood flow to the follicle and may counteract the effects of **DHT** (dihydrotestosterone) on hair follicles. The evidence is promising but not definitive. It's found in many anti-thinning shampoos and tonics.

### Peptides and Botanicals

**Peptides** are short chains of amino acids that can signal the body to produce more collagen or support follicle health. **Saw palmetto**, **pumpkin seed oil**, and **rosemary oil** have some evidence for supporting hair growth, though clinical data varies.

### Natural Oils

- **Castor oil** — heavy, occlusive, seals in moisture. Popular for edges and dry scalps.
- **Jojoba oil** — mimics sebum closely, lightweight, good for balancing oily and dry scalps.
- **Tea tree oil** — antimicrobial and antifungal properties, useful for mild scalp infections at 1-5% concentration. **Must be diluted** — undiluted tea tree oil can cause contact dermatitis.

> I'm often asked about miracle ingredients. The truth is, there are no miracles — just good science applied consistently. The best ingredient is the one your client will actually use regularly.

## Treatment Modalities

### Scalp Steaming

Steam opens the follicles, softens scale and build-up, and **improves product absorption**. It's relaxing for the client and can be incorporated into a luxury scalp ritual. Use for 5-10 minutes before applying treatment products. Contraindicated for clients with active inflammation or infection.

### Exfoliation

Physical or chemical exfoliation removes dead skin cells, product build-up, and excess sebum. **Physical** (scrubs with fine granules) should be gentle — no aggressive scrubbing. **Chemical** (salicylic acid, glycolic acid) is often more effective and less traumatic to the scalp.

### LED Therapy

**Red light (630-660nm)** reduces inflammation and may support follicle activity. **Near-infrared (830-850nm)** penetrates deeper. LED therapy is non-invasive and has growing evidence for supporting hair regrowth when used consistently. Sessions typically run 15-20 minutes.

### Scalp Massage

Proper scalp massage technique involves slow, firm circular movements using the **pads of the fingers** (never nails). Benefits include improved blood circulation, stress reduction, and better product distribution. Massage for 3-5 minutes during treatment application.

## Contraindications to Know

- **Open wounds or broken skin** — do not apply active ingredients
- **Active infection** — refer, do not treat
- **Pregnancy** — check ingredient safety (some essential oils and high-concentration actives are contraindicated)
- **Allergy history** — always patch test new products 48 hours before use
- **Medication interactions** — clients on blood thinners should avoid vigorous scalp massage

## Key Takeaways

- Match active ingredients to the condition: salicylic acid for scale, niacinamide for inflammation, caffeine for circulation
- Always dilute essential oils and patch test new products
- Steaming and massage enhance product absorption and client experience
- Know your contraindications — they protect you and your clients
- Consistency matters more than intensity in scalp treatment

## Reflection

A client presents with a flaky, slightly itchy scalp and says they've tried "everything" from the chemist. Design a simple in-salon scalp treatment using the ingredients and techniques from this lesson. What would you include, and in what order?

lessons.description: Understanding ethnic variations and how to assess hair health
lessons.content:
## Why Ethnic Hair Knowledge Matters

Hair is beautifully diverse. But that diversity means a one-size-fits-all approach to hair care is not just unhelpful — it can be actively harmful. Understanding how hair differs across ethnicities isn't just cultural sensitivity (though it is that too). It's **clinical necessity**.

## Hair Types in Detail

### Asian Hair

**Asian hair** typically has a **round cross-section**, producing straight strands with high tensile strength. Key characteristics:

- Highest density of any hair type (up to 100,000+ follicles)
- Thick individual strands with a wide medulla
- Cuticle layers are tightly packed — gives excellent shine but resists chemical penetration
- Growth rate is generally the fastest of any ethnic group (~1.3cm per month)
- Lower risk of breakage but higher susceptibility to weight-related traction at the root

### European Hair

The most variable hair type, ranging from fine and straight to thick and curly. **Oval cross-section** produces waves. Key points:

- Medium density (approximately 80,000-100,000 follicles)
- Most varied in colour, from platinum blonde to deepest brown
- Moderate susceptibility to both chemical and physical damage
- Fine European hair is particularly vulnerable to traction and heat damage

### Afro-textured Hair

**Flat, elliptical cross-section** producing tight coils and curls. This hair type requires specific understanding:

- **Lowest tensile strength** of all hair types — breaks under less force
- Sebum travels very slowly down the spiral shaft, making it the **driest hair type**
- Higher susceptibility to **breakage, dryness, and traction damage**
- Shrinkage can mask true length by 50-75%
- Chemical relaxers are widely used but carry significant damage risk with repeated application

> I've seen too many stylists treat Afro-textured hair like European hair with more product. That approach causes damage. Every hair type deserves to be understood on its own terms, not forced into someone else's framework.

## Tension Zones and Traction Risk

**Tension zones** are areas of the scalp where hair is under the greatest mechanical stress from styling. Recognising these zones is critical for preventing **traction alopecia**.

- **Frontal hairline** — the most common area for traction damage, especially from tight ponytails, slicked-back styles, and lace-front wig adhesive
- **Temporal regions** — braids, cornrows, and tight updos create sustained tension here
- **Nape** — hair wraps, low buns, and certain protective styles can stress this area
- **Crown** — heavy extensions and weaves distribute weight here

**Growth patterns** also matter: cowlicks, whorls, and natural parting lines create areas where hair grows in different directions. Styling against these patterns increases tension.

## Practical Assessment Skills

### Porosity Testing

Place a clean, product-free strand in a glass of room-temperature water:
- **Floats on surface** = low porosity (intact cuticle, resists moisture)
- **Sinks slowly** = normal porosity (balanced absorption)
- **Sinks quickly** = high porosity (damaged or lifted cuticle, absorbs but doesn't retain)

### Elasticity Testing

Take a single wet hair strand and gently stretch:
- **Stretches 30% and springs back** = healthy elasticity
- **Snaps with minimal stretch** = needs protein
- **Stretches without springing back** = needs moisture

> Product build-up can make low-porosity hair test as normal, and silicone coating can make high-porosity hair seem fine. Always test on freshly clarified hair for accurate results.

## Key Takeaways

- Hair type determines care approach — never apply a one-size-fits-all method
- Afro-textured hair is the most fragile and requires the most gentle handling
- Tension zones vary by styling habit — identify them early to prevent traction alopecia
- Porosity and elasticity testing gives you actionable, objective data
- Always test on clean, product-free hair for accurate results

## Reflection

Consider your current client base. Which hair types do you see most often, and are there any where you feel less confident in your approach? What would you change about your consultation process to better serve diverse hair types?

lessons.title: Internal factors affecting hair health
lessons.description: From iron deficiency to cortisol — what's happening inside
lessons.content:
## The Inside Story

Here's a truth that changes how you think about hair: **hair is non-essential tissue**. Your body considers it expendable. When resources are scarce — whether nutrients, hormones, or energy — hair is one of the first things to suffer. This makes hair a surprisingly sensitive barometer of overall health.

Today's lesson connects what's happening inside the body to what you see on the scalp and in the hair. This knowledge won't make you a doctor, but it will make you a far more perceptive professional.

## Nutritional Factors

Several key nutrients are essential for healthy hair growth:

### Iron

**Iron deficiency** is the most common nutritional cause of hair shedding, particularly in women. Iron supports the production of haemoglobin, which carries oxygen to follicle cells. Low iron doesn't just cause anaemia — subclinical deficiency (ferritin below 40-70 ng/mL) can trigger diffuse shedding even when blood counts look normal.

### Zinc

**Zinc** plays a role in cell division and protein synthesis. Deficiency can cause diffuse hair loss and changes in hair texture. It's particularly relevant for clients on restricted diets or with digestive conditions.

### Vitamin D3

Emerging research links **Vitamin D3 deficiency** to hair follicle cycling problems and alopecia areata. Many people in the UK are deficient, particularly during winter months.

### B12 and Folate

**B12 deficiency** can cause premature greying and diffuse hair loss. It's common in vegans, vegetarians, and older adults with reduced absorption.

### Protein

Hair is made of **keratin**, a protein. Inadequate dietary protein — common in crash diets, restrictive eating, and some vegan diets without proper planning — directly limits the body's ability to produce healthy hair.

### Biotin

The most marketed hair supplement, but **biotin deficiency is actually rare**. Supplementation only helps if there's a genuine deficiency. For most people, biotin supplements are expensive urine.

> When a client asks me about supplements, I always say: test first, supplement second. Taking random vitamins without knowing your baseline is guesswork, and some supplements can actually interfere with each other or with medications.

## Hormonal Factors

### DHT and Pattern Hair Loss

**Dihydrotestosterone (DHT)** is the primary hormonal driver of **androgenetic alopecia** (pattern hair loss) in both men and women. DHT miniaturises sensitive follicles over time, producing progressively finer, shorter hairs until the follicle stops producing visible hair entirely.

### Menopause and Oestrogen Decline

As oestrogen levels fall during menopause, the relative influence of androgens increases. Many women notice diffuse thinning, changes in hair texture, and slower growth during and after menopause.

### PCOS

**Polycystic ovary syndrome** produces elevated androgens, which can cause both scalp hair thinning and unwanted facial/body hair growth. If a young woman presents with thinning hair, acne, and irregular periods, PCOS should be considered.

### Postpartum Telogen Effluvium

During pregnancy, elevated oestrogen extends the anagen phase — hair feels thicker and fuller. After birth, oestrogen drops sharply, pushing a large proportion of hair into telogen simultaneously. The resulting shedding typically begins 2-4 months postpartum and can be dramatic but is almost always temporary.

### Thyroid Disorders

Both **hypothyroidism** and **hyperthyroidism** affect hair. Hypothyroidism typically causes diffuse thinning, dry, brittle hair, and sometimes loss of the outer third of the eyebrow. Hyperthyroidism causes fine, soft hair that sheds easily.

## Lifestyle Factors

- **Chronic stress** elevates cortisol, which can push follicles from anagen into telogen. Stress-related hair loss typically appears 2-3 months after the stressful period.
- **Poor sleep** disrupts growth hormone release and scalp repair processes.
- **Gut health** — emerging research suggests gut inflammation may influence systemic inflammation affecting follicles.
- **Smoking** reduces blood flow to the scalp and introduces oxidative stress to follicle cells.
- **Crash diets** are a common trigger for telogen effluvium — rapid weight loss signals the body to conserve resources.

## Key Takeaways

- Hair is non-essential tissue — it's the first to suffer when the body is stressed or depleted
- Iron deficiency is the most common nutritional cause of hair shedding
- DHT is the hormonal driver of pattern hair loss in both sexes
- Postpartum shedding is dramatic but temporary — reassure clients
- Always recommend testing before supplementation

## Reflection

A client in her late 40s mentions her hair has been thinning for the past year, she's been feeling tired, and her periods have become irregular. What internal factors might be contributing, and what would you suggest as a next step?

lessons.description: From intake to follow-up — running professional consultations
lessons.content:
## The Art and Science of Consultation

A good consultation is where science meets empathy. It's where you gather the information you need to help, while making the client feel heard, respected, and safe. Today we bring together everything you've learned this week into a practical consultation framework.

> The consultation is your most powerful tool. It's not just information gathering — it's the moment you build or break trust. Get this right, and everything else follows.

## The Four-Part Framework

Every consultation should follow this structure, regardless of the presenting concern:

### 1. History Taking

Start with **open questions** to let the client tell their story:
- "What brings you in today?"
- "When did you first notice this?"
- "What have you tried so far?"

Then move to **specific questions** to fill in the clinical picture:
- Medical history (conditions, surgeries, hospitalisations)
- Family history (pattern hair loss, autoimmune conditions)
- Medications (including supplements and over-the-counter products)
- Lifestyle factors (stress, sleep, diet, exercise)
- Hormonal history (menstrual cycle, pregnancy, menopause)
- Allergies (products, ingredients, sensitivities)

### 2. Examination

Using the systematic examination protocol from Day 3:
- Visual inspection of the scalp (colour, scale, distribution of any changes)
- Palpation (texture, tenderness)
- Pattern mapping (where is the concern — diffuse, patchy, marginal?)
- Hair shaft assessment (porosity, elasticity, condition)
- Photography for baseline documentation

### 3. Assessment

Based on history and examination, form a **working hypothesis** — not a diagnosis. Use language like:
- "Based on what I'm seeing, this looks consistent with..."
- "I think what may be happening is..."
- "I'd like to suggest..."

### 4. Plan

Every consultation should end with a **clear, written plan** that includes:
- What you're going to do (treatments, product recommendations)
- What the client should do at home
- Timeline for expected results (always realistic)
- When to come back for review
- Whether a referral is recommended

## Building Rapport

**Body language matters** as much as words:
- Sit at the same level as your client, not standing over them
- Make eye contact when they're speaking
- Use their name
- Mirror their energy — if they're anxious, be calm and steady
- Never rush, even when you're busy

**Acknowledge emotions** before offering information. A client who says "I'm terrified I'm going bald" doesn't need statistics first — they need to hear "I understand this is really worrying for you."

## Allergy Testing

For any new product application, particularly colour or chemical services:
- Apply a small amount behind the ear or on the inner elbow
- Wait **48 hours** minimum
- Document the test, the product used, and the result
- If there's any reaction (redness, swelling, itching), do not proceed

## Progress Monitoring

**Standardised photography** is essential:
- Same lighting, same angles, same distance every time
- Part the hair in the same location
- Include a date stamp or reference card in the image
- Store securely and share only with the client's consent

## Managing Expectations

Hair improvement is slow. Set expectations clearly:
- "We should see early signs of change in 3-4 months"
- "Full results typically take 6-12 months"
- "Some shedding may continue or even temporarily increase before improvement"
- "Progress is often subtle — that's why photos matter"

## Key Takeaways

- Every consultation follows four steps: History, Examination, Assessment, Plan
- Start with open questions, then narrow to specifics
- Rapport comes from genuine attention, appropriate body language, and emotional validation
- Always patch test new products 48 hours before use
- Standardised photography tracks progress objectively
- Set realistic timelines — hair changes are measured in months, not weeks

## Reflection

Design your ideal consultation form. What sections would it include? How would you structure it to flow naturally in a conversation rather than feeling like an interrogation?

lessons.content:
## From Knowledge to Practice

You've spent seven days building a deep understanding of hair science, scalp conditions, and clinical skills. Today is about turning that knowledge into a sustainable, profitable part of your business — while maintaining the highest ethical standards.

## Creating Scalp-Focused Services

Your trichology knowledge opens up entirely new service categories. Here's how to build them:

### The Scalp Health Consultation (30 min)

A standalone service using everything you've learned:
- Client history and lifestyle screening
- Scalp examination with magnification
- Porosity and elasticity testing
- Written recommendations and plan
- Baseline photography

**Pricing guide:** Position this as a premium service. You're offering expertise, not just time. Price at £45-£75 depending on your market. It's the entry point to ongoing care.

### The Luxury Scalp Ritual (45-60 min)

A treatment service that combines clinical benefit with relaxation:
1. Scalp analysis and discussion
2. Gentle cleanse with condition-appropriate shampoo
3. Steam treatment (5-10 minutes)
4. Chemical or physical exfoliation
5. Treatment mask or serum application
6. Scalp massage (5-7 minutes)
7. Rinse and style

**Pricing guide:** £55-£95 as a standalone, or £35-£55 as an add-on to existing services. Use professional-grade products and explain what each step does — education is part of the experience.

### The Scalp Care Add-On (15-20 min)

A quick version that slots into existing appointments:
- Quick scalp check and discussion
- Targeted treatment application
- Brief massage

**Pricing guide:** £15-£30 as an upgrade. Low barrier for clients to try, high potential for conversion to full consultations.

> I always tell my students: don't sell treatments. Sell understanding. When a client understands what's happening with their scalp and why your recommendation matters, the service sells itself.

## Safe Language for Marketing

This is critical. You must market your services without making medical claims:

**Do say:**
- "Scalp health assessment"
- "I've noticed some changes in..."
- "Our scalp ritual promotes a healthy scalp environment"
- "Supporting your scalp's natural balance"

**Don't say:**
- "Scalp diagnosis" (you're not diagnosing)
- "This treatment cures..." (you're not curing)
- "Guaranteed regrowth" (no treatment guarantees this)
- "Clinical treatment" (unless you have clinical qualifications)

## Building Ongoing Relationships

### Consultation Forms

Use the forms from Day 7 at every appointment. They demonstrate professionalism, track progress, and protect you legally.

### Progress Photography

Nothing builds trust like visible evidence of improvement. Take photos at every visit using consistent methods. Share them with the client to reinforce the value of continuing.

### Client Education

Teach your clients what you know — at an appropriate level. When clients understand *why* a product or technique matters, they're more likely to follow through and return.

### Referral Relationships

Build connections with local trichologists and dermatologists. When you refer well, those professionals refer back to you. Your willingness to refer shows integrity and builds your reputation.

## Ethical Marketing

All marketing materials should include:
- Clear descriptions of what services include
- Realistic expectations for outcomes
- Your qualifications and training
- Appropriate disclaimers ("This service does not replace medical advice")
- Before/after photos only with client consent and honest representation

## Continuing Professional Development

Trichology is a field that evolves. Commit to:
- Annual refresher training
- Staying current with ingredient research
- Joining professional associations
- Building case study experience
- Mentoring and peer learning

## Key Takeaways

- Create tiered services: consultation, full ritual, and quick add-on
- Price based on expertise and value, not just time
- Use safe, non-medical language in all marketing
- Progress photography builds trust and demonstrates value
- Building referral relationships strengthens your professional standing
- Continue learning — trichology knowledge evolves constantly

## Reflection

Draft a one-paragraph description of a scalp health service for your website or social media. Does it accurately represent what you offer without making claims beyond your scope? How would a potential client feel reading it?

lessons.title: The structured examination protocol
lessons.description: A step-by-step approach to scalp assessment
lessons.content:
## Why Structure Matters

Every experienced practitioner develops their own way of examining a scalp. But without a **structured protocol**, it's easy to miss subtle findings — especially when the presenting concern is obvious and your attention is drawn to it immediately.

A systematic approach ensures you examine the **entire scalp**, not just the area the client points to. Some of the most important findings are in areas the client hasn't noticed.

## The Four-Step Examination Protocol

### Step 1: Visual Inspection

Before you touch anything, **look**. Observe the scalp under good, consistent lighting (ideally daylight or a daylight-balanced lamp).

Assess:
- **Colour** — Is there erythema (redness)? Is it diffuse or localised? Are there any violaceous (purple-tinged) areas suggesting inflammation?
- **Scale** — Is there scaling? What type? Dry and white (dandruff/psoriasis), greasy and yellow (seb derm), adherent and cast-like (pityriasis amiantacea)?
- **Distribution** — Is the concern diffuse (all over), patchy (localised areas), or marginal (at the hairline)?
- **Hair density** — Can you see the scalp more than expected? Is the part line widening? Are there areas of complete loss?
- **Follicular openings** — Are follicular openings visible? (Absent openings suggest scarring alopecia.)

### Step 2: Palpation

Gently palpate the scalp with your fingertips:
- **Texture** — Does the scalp feel smooth, rough, thickened, or thinned?
- **Tenderness** — Does the client experience pain when you touch certain areas? Tenderness can indicate inflammation.
- **Temperature** — Localised warmth suggests active inflammation.
- **Mobility** — A healthy scalp moves freely over the skull. Reduced mobility may suggest fibrosis.

### Step 3: Pattern Mapping

Document where you're finding changes using a scalp map:
- **Diffuse** — changes across the entire scalp (common in telogen effluvium, female pattern hair loss)
- **Patchy** — well-defined areas of change (alopecia areata, tinea capitis, scarring alopecias)
- **Marginal** — changes at the hairline (traction alopecia, frontal fibrosing alopecia)
- **Vertex/crown** — changes at the top of the head (male pattern, some female pattern)

### Step 4: Documentation

Record everything you find, even negative findings ("no scale observed", "no tenderness"). Use standardised photography and a consistent recording format.

> I teach my students that the examination findings you don't write down are the ones that come back to haunt you. Document everything — it protects your client, protects you, and gives you the data to track change over time.

## Common Examination Pitfalls

- **Confirmation bias** — seeing what you expect to see. Always examine the full scalp, even when the client points to one area.
- **Ignoring the hairline** — subtle recession at the frontal or temporal hairline is easy to miss.
- **Poor lighting** — erythema and subtle scale can be invisible under salon fluorescents.
- **Rushing** — a thorough examination takes 5-10 minutes. Don't shortcut it.

## Key Takeaways

- A structured protocol (look, touch, map, document) ensures you miss nothing
- Always examine the full scalp, not just the area of concern
- Document negative findings as well as positive ones
- Good lighting is essential for accurate visual assessment
- Pattern mapping helps guide your differential diagnosis

## Reflection

Think about your current examination process. Do you follow the same steps every time, or does it vary depending on the client? What would you add or change to make your examination more systematic?

lessons.title: Trichoscopy fundamentals
lessons.description: What to look for under magnification
lessons.content:
## Seeing What the Eye Cannot

**Trichoscopy** — dermoscopy applied to the scalp — is the single most valuable diagnostic tool in modern trichology practice. It reveals patterns, structures, and changes that are invisible to the naked eye, and it transforms your ability to distinguish between conditions that look similar clinically.

You don't need expensive equipment to start. A basic dermatoscope with 10x magnification and polarised light will reveal most of the features discussed in this lesson. As you advance, video trichoscopy at higher magnifications (20-70x) allows detailed analysis and client-facing education.

## Essential Trichoscopic Features

### Follicular Unit Density

A healthy scalp shows **consistent follicular unit density** — clusters of 1-4 hairs emerging from each follicular unit. In androgenetic alopecia, you'll see **miniaturisation**: some units producing thin, vellus-like hairs instead of thick terminal hairs. The ratio of thin to thick hairs (**hair diameter diversity**) is one of the most reliable trichoscopic signs of pattern hair loss.

### Peripilar Signs

**Peripilar casts** — white or yellowish concentric scales around the hair shaft at the scalp surface — are seen in several conditions:
- Brown peripilar casts in frontal fibrosing alopecia
- White peripilar scale in lichen planopilaris
- Greasy peripilar scale in seborrhoeic dermatitis

### Vascular Patterns

The scalp has characteristic blood vessel patterns visible under trichoscopy:
- **Simple red loops** — normal finding
- **Twisted or coiled loops** — suggests psoriasis
- **Arborising (tree-like) vessels** — seen in some inflammatory conditions
- **Absent vasculature** — may indicate scarring

### Yellow and Black Dots

- **Yellow dots** — follicular openings filled with sebum and keratin. Classic finding in **alopecia areata** but also seen in androgenetic alopecia.
- **Black dots** — broken hairs at the scalp surface. Seen in **alopecia areata** (cadaverised hairs), **tinea capitis**, and **trichotillomania**.

### Exclamation Mark Hairs

Short, broken hairs that taper at the base — thinner at the root than the tip, like an exclamation mark. This is a **pathognomonic sign of alopecia areata**, meaning it's virtually diagnostic when present.

> Learning trichoscopy is like learning a new language. At first, everything looks the same. But with practice, you start seeing patterns you can't unsee. Keep a library of images — your own and from reference texts — and compare constantly.

## Building Your Visual Library

The key to trichoscopic competence is **pattern recognition**, and that comes from exposure:
- Photograph every trichoscopic finding you encounter
- Compare your images to published atlases and case studies
- Attend workshops and conferences where live trichoscopy is demonstrated
- Practice on every client, even those without complaints — you need to know what normal looks like before you can reliably spot abnormal

## Key Takeaways

- Trichoscopy reveals diagnostic features invisible to the naked eye
- Hair diameter diversity is the key trichoscopic sign of pattern hair loss
- Yellow dots, black dots, and exclamation mark hairs each point to specific conditions
- Vascular patterns help differentiate inflammatory conditions
- Build your visual library through consistent practice and documentation

## Reflection

If you have access to a dermatoscope, examine your own scalp or a willing colleague's. What follicular patterns and vascular features can you identify? How does magnified appearance compare to what you see with the naked eye?

lessons.title: Scarring vs non-scarring alopecia
lessons.description: The most critical distinction in hair loss assessment
lessons.content:
## The Most Important Question

When you encounter hair loss, the first clinical question you must answer is: **is this scarring or non-scarring?** This distinction determines urgency, prognosis, and whether the client needs immediate medical referral.

**Scarring (cicatricial) alopecias** destroy the hair follicle permanently. The follicle is replaced by fibrous tissue. Once a follicle is scarred, it cannot regrow hair. Early detection and treatment can halt progression, but lost follicles cannot be recovered.

**Non-scarring alopecias** leave the follicle intact. Even in conditions like alopecia areata where hair loss is complete, the follicular structure remains and regrowth is possible.

## How to Tell the Difference

### Clinical Features

**Signs of scarring:**
- Smooth, shiny scalp surface where follicular openings are **absent**
- Scalp may feel firmer or less mobile in affected areas
- Perifollicular erythema (redness around follicles) in active disease
- Perifollicular scale or casts at the margins of loss
- Loss of follicular markings (the scalp looks "blank")

**Signs of non-scarring:**
- Follicular openings are **preserved** (you can see pores)
- Scalp texture and mobility are normal
- Smooth patches without surrounding inflammation (alopecia areata)
- Diffuse thinning with preserved follicular pattern (TE, AGA)

### Key Scarring Alopecias to Recognise

**Lichen Planopilaris (LPP):**
- Perifollicular erythema and scale
- Patchy loss, often at the crown or vertex
- Itching or tenderness may be present
- Trichoscopy shows peripilar casts and loss of follicular openings

**Frontal Fibrosing Alopecia (FFA):**
- Symmetrical recession of the frontal hairline
- Loss of eyebrows (often the first sign)
- Perifollicular redness at the active margin
- Lone hairs may remain within the band of loss

**Central Centrifugal Cicatricial Alopecia (CCCA):**
- Primarily affects women of African descent
- Begins at the crown/vertex and spreads outward
- Often associated with heat styling and chemical processing, though genetics play a role
- Early perifollicular inflammation progresses to smooth, scarred scalp

**Discoid Lupus Erythematosus:**
- Well-defined, disc-shaped patches
- Redness, scale, follicular plugging, and eventual scarring
- May leave hypopigmented (lighter) or hyperpigmented (darker) patches
- Systemic lupus should be investigated

> When I suspect scarring alopecia, I treat it as urgent. The window for preserving follicles is limited. I would rather refer a non-urgent case urgently than miss an early scarring process. A dermatologist will never criticise you for erring on the side of caution.

## The Referral Decision

**Refer urgently when:**
- Follicular openings are absent in the area of loss
- There is active inflammation at the margins (redness, scale, tenderness)
- The client reports scalp pain or burning
- Hair loss is progressing rapidly

**Refer routinely when:**
- You suspect non-scarring alopecia that isn't responding to treatment
- The client wants medical investigation for systemic causes
- You're uncertain about the classification

## Key Takeaways

- The scarring vs non-scarring distinction is the most important clinical question in hair loss
- Absent follicular openings = scarring = urgent referral
- Know the key scarring conditions: LPP, FFA, CCCA, discoid lupus
- When in doubt, refer — it's better to be cautious than to miss early scarring
- Early intervention in scarring alopecia can preserve remaining follicles

## Reflection

A client presents with a band of hair loss across the frontal hairline with loss of eyebrows. The skin in the affected area looks smooth and slightly shiny. What condition does this suggest, and what would your immediate next step be?

resources.title: Scarring vs Non-Scarring Decision Framework
resources.content:
## Scarring vs Non-Scarring Alopecia

### Step 1: Check Follicular Openings
- **Present** → Likely non-scarring → Proceed to Step 2
- **Absent** → Likely scarring → **Refer urgently**

### Step 2: Assess Inflammation
- **Perifollicular redness/scale at margins** → Active scarring process → **Refer urgently**
- **No inflammation** → Likely non-scarring → Proceed to assessment

### Step 3: Pattern Recognition
| Pattern | Likely Condition | Scarring? |
|---------|-----------------|----------|
| Smooth round patches, no inflammation | Alopecia areata | No |
| Diffuse thinning, widening part | AGA / TE | No |
| Frontal recession + eyebrow loss | FFA | **Yes** |
| Crown spreading outward | CCCA | **Yes** |
| Patchy with perifollicular scale | LPP | **Yes** |
| Disc-shaped with follicular plugging | Discoid lupus | **Yes** |

### Red Flags for Urgent Referral
- Scalp pain or burning sensation
- Rapidly progressing loss
- Shiny, smooth scalp surface
- Loss of follicular markings

lessons.title: Overlapping presentations
lessons.description: When TE meets FPHL, when psoriasis mimics dermatitis
lessons.content:
## Real Life Doesn't Read Textbooks

In clinical practice, textbook presentations are the exception, not the rule. Most clients present with **overlapping conditions** — multiple factors contributing simultaneously. Your job is to untangle the picture, identify the primary driver, and create a prioritised plan.

## Common Overlaps

### Telogen Effluvium + Female Pattern Hair Loss

This is the **most common combination** you'll encounter. A woman with underlying FPHL (genetic predisposition to progressive thinning) experiences a trigger — stress, illness, medication change, postpartum hormone shift — that pushes a large number of hairs into telogen.

The result: dramatic shedding on top of existing thinning. The client is terrified because the shedding is acute, but the underlying thinning has been progressing silently for years.

**How to distinguish:**
- TE shedding is **diffuse** and involves full-length hairs with white bulbs (club hairs)
- FPHL shows **miniaturisation** on trichoscopy — fine, thin hairs alongside normal ones
- TE typically begins 2-3 months after a trigger and resolves within 6-9 months
- FPHL is progressive and doesn't resolve spontaneously

**Clinical approach:**
- Address the TE trigger first (it's more distressing and more immediately treatable)
- Reassure that the acute shedding will resolve
- Then address the underlying FPHL as a separate, ongoing management plan

### Seborrhoeic Dermatitis vs Psoriasis

Both cause scale and redness on the scalp. Both can itch. Both are chronic and relapsing. But the treatment approach differs.

**Key differences:**
- Seb derm scale is **greasy and yellowish**; psoriasis scale is **dry and silvery**
- Seb derm favours the **hairline, ears, and nasolabial folds**; psoriasis plaques are **well-defined with sharp borders**
- Psoriasis often extends **beyond the hairline onto the forehead**
- Seb derm responds to **antifungals** (ketoconazole); psoriasis requires **anti-inflammatory** approaches

### Contact Dermatitis vs Seborrhoeic Dermatitis

Contact dermatitis from hair products can mimic seb derm. The key question: **has the client recently changed products?** If symptoms appeared within days of trying a new shampoo, colour, or styling product, contact dermatitis is likely.

**Distinguishing features:**
- Contact dermatitis distribution follows the **area of product application**
- It's typically more **acutely itchy** and may have vesicles (tiny blisters)
- Removal of the offending product leads to improvement

### Diffuse Alopecia Areata vs Telogen Effluvium

Both cause diffuse shedding without obvious patches. This is a genuinely difficult differential.

**Clues favouring alopecia areata:**
- **Exclamation mark hairs** on trichoscopy
- **Yellow dots** on trichoscopy
- No identifiable trigger
- Personal or family history of autoimmune conditions
- Nail changes (pitting, ridging)

**Clues favouring TE:**
- Clear temporal relationship to a trigger
- Full-length shed hairs with intact bulbs
- No trichoscopic signs of AA

> When I'm faced with an overlap, I write out each possible condition separately, list the evidence for and against each one, and then rank them by likelihood. It sounds formal, but it stops you from getting overwhelmed by complexity.

## Documentation of Complex Cases

When presentations overlap, your documentation becomes even more important:
- Record your differential diagnoses in order of likelihood
- Note the evidence for and against each
- Document your reasoning for the chosen treatment approach
- Set clear review points to reassess

## Key Takeaways

- Most real-world presentations involve overlapping conditions
- TE on FPHL is the most common overlap — address the acute trigger first, then manage the chronic condition
- Seb derm and psoriasis look similar but respond to different treatments
- Always ask about recent product changes when you see contact dermatitis patterns
- Document your differential reasoning — it's your clinical audit trail

## Reflection

A woman in her early 30s presents with 3 months of increased shedding. She had COVID-19 four months ago. On trichoscopy, you notice both full-length shed hairs and some areas of hair diameter diversity. What might be happening, and how would you explain it to the client?

lessons.title: Clinical documentation best practices
lessons.description: What to record, how to photograph, and why it matters
lessons.content:
## Documentation as a Clinical Tool

Documentation isn't paperwork — it's a clinical tool. Good records allow you to track changes over time, justify your decisions, communicate with colleagues, and protect yourself professionally. In trichology, where changes happen over months, documentation is often the only way to demonstrate whether a treatment is working.

## Standardised Photography

Photography is your most powerful documentation tool in trichology practice.

### Setting Up Consistent Photos

- **Lighting:** Use the same light source every time. Daylight is ideal, but consistent artificial light works if you can't access natural light. Avoid mixed lighting.
- **Distance:** Maintain the same distance for each shot. A fixed camera mount or tripod helps.
- **Angles:** Use a minimum of 5 standard views: top (vertex), front, left profile, right profile, and back.
- **Parting:** Part the hair in the same location each time. Consider marking the part line description in the client record.
- **Reference:** Include a date card or reference marker in each image.
- **Background:** Use a plain, neutral background when possible.

### What to Photograph

- Baseline images at the first consultation (even if the client doesn't have a hair concern)
- The area(s) of concern at each visit
- Trichoscopy images of key findings
- Any changes you notice, even subtle ones

### Storage and Consent

- Store images securely, in compliance with GDPR
- Obtain written consent for photography and specify how images will be used
- Never share client images without explicit consent
- Consider encrypted cloud storage with client-specific folders

## Consultation Records

Every consultation should generate a written record including:

### The SOAP Format

A widely used clinical documentation framework:

- **S (Subjective):** What the client tells you — their concerns, symptoms, history
- **O (Objective):** What you observe — examination findings, trichoscopy results, test outcomes
- **A (Assessment):** Your clinical interpretation — working hypothesis, differential diagnoses
- **P (Plan):** What happens next — treatments, recommendations, referrals, review dates

> I've been using SOAP notes for twenty years, and they've saved me more than once. When a client comes back six months later and you can't remember the specifics, your notes tell the story. When a dermatologist asks what you've observed, your notes speak clearly.

## Progress Tracking

Design a simple tracking system that works for your practice:

- **Quantitative measures:** Hair density scores from trichoscopy, pull test results, shed hair counts
- **Qualitative measures:** Client-reported satisfaction, styling observations, quality of life impact
- **Visual comparison:** Side-by-side photos from different dates
- **Treatment compliance:** Is the client following the plan? What barriers exist?

## Digital Tools

Several digital tools support trichology documentation:
- **Canfield VISIA** and **FotoFinder** — professional trichology imaging systems
- **Standard dermatoscope apps** — connect to your phone for basic trichoscopy images
- **Practice management software** — many systems include photo storage and clinical notes
- **Simple solutions** — even a consistent folder structure on a secure device works

## Key Takeaways

- Standardised photography with consistent lighting, angles, and distance is essential
- Use the SOAP format for clinical notes: Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan
- Document negative findings as well as positive ones
- Obtain written consent for all photography and comply with GDPR
- Simple, consistent documentation systems are better than complex ones you won't use

## Reflection

Review your current documentation practices. If a client came back in 12 months and you needed to compare their scalp condition to today, would your current records allow that? What one change would make the biggest improvement?

lessons.content:
## Building Your Professional Network

No trichologist works alone. Your effectiveness depends not just on your own skills, but on your ability to involve the right specialists at the right time. A strong referral network transforms you from a solo practitioner into a valued member of a multi-disciplinary team.

## When to Refer

### Urgent Referral (Within Days)

- **Suspected scarring alopecia** — any presentation with absent follicular openings and active margin inflammation
- **Rapidly progressive hair loss** — significant change over weeks rather than months
- **Scalp pain with hair loss** — "trichodynia" with visible changes suggests active inflammatory process
- **Suspected infection with systemic symptoms** — fever, spreading redness, lymph node swelling
- **Sudden onset of widespread alopecia areata** — especially in children

### Routine Referral (Within Weeks)

- **Conditions not responding to your treatment** after an appropriate trial period (typically 3-6 months)
- **Suspected hormonal or systemic causes** requiring blood investigation
- **Complex presentations** where your differential diagnosis is uncertain
- **Client request** — the client wants medical assessment regardless of your findings
- **Psychological impact** — when hair loss is significantly affecting mental health

## Who to Refer To

- **Dermatologist** — for diagnosis and medical treatment of scalp conditions, scarring alopecias, and conditions requiring biopsy
- **GP** — for blood tests, general health investigation, and onward referral to specialists
- **Endocrinologist** — for hormonal investigations (PCOS, thyroid disorders, adrenal conditions)
- **Nutritionist/Dietitian** — for comprehensive dietary assessment and supplementation guidance
- **Psychologist/Counsellor** — for clients experiencing significant psychological distress, trichotillomania, or body dysmorphia

## Writing an Effective Referral

A good referral letter should be concise, professional, and include everything the receiving clinician needs.

### Structure

1. **Your details** — name, qualifications, practice address, contact information
2. **Client details** — name, date of birth, contact information (with consent)
3. **Reason for referral** — one clear sentence stating why you're referring
4. **History** — brief relevant history including timeline, triggers, and treatments tried
5. **Examination findings** — your key observations and trichoscopy findings
6. **Your assessment** — your working hypothesis and concerns
7. **What you're asking for** — specific request (diagnosis, investigation, treatment, or shared care)

> The referrals that get taken seriously are the ones that show you've done your homework. A letter that says "client has hair loss, please assess" will go to the bottom of the pile. A letter that says "I'm concerned about a possible scarring process — absent follicular openings at the vertex with perifollicular erythema, progressing over 6 months" gets attention.

## Maintaining the Relationship

Referral doesn't mean handover. Your role continues:

- **Communicate clearly** with the client about why you're referring and what to expect
- **Provide a copy** of your referral letter to the client
- **Continue supportive care** — scalp treatments, product advice, emotional support
- **Request feedback** from the specialist (with client consent) to inform your ongoing care
- **Coordinate treatment plans** — your scalp treatments may complement medical treatment

## Building Referral Relationships

- Introduce yourself to local dermatologists and GPs — a brief letter or email explaining your services
- Offer to provide complementary care for their patients
- Send professional referral letters that demonstrate your competence
- Attend multi-disciplinary events and conferences
- Over time, specialists who trust your judgement will refer clients back to you

## Key Takeaways

- Know the difference between urgent and routine referral situations
- Match the referral to the right specialist (dermatologist, GP, endocrinologist, psychologist)
- A well-structured referral letter with clear findings gets better responses
- Referral doesn't mean you step away — continue your supportive role
- Building professional relationships with specialists strengthens your practice

## Reflection

Draft a referral letter for a hypothetical client with a 6-month history of progressive frontal hairline recession and loss of eyebrows. What findings would you include, and what specifically would you ask the dermatologist to assess?

lessons.description: Dandruff, dermatitis, psoriasis, and contact reactions
lessons.content:
## Your Unique Position

As a stylist, you see more scalps in a week than most GPs do in a month. You're in a unique position — not to diagnose, but to **recognise** and **guide**. This lesson gives you the visual vocabulary to identify the most common conditions your clients walk in with.

## The Big Four

### Dandruff (Pityriasis Capitis)

The condition you'll see most often. **Dandruff** shows as white or greyish **dry flakes** on the scalp and shoulders. It's generally not inflamed — the skin underneath looks normal. Most clients manage it themselves with over-the-counter shampoos, but persistent dandruff that doesn't respond may be mild seborrhoeic dermatitis.

**What it looks like:** Fine white flakes, dry texture, minimal redness
**How the client feels:** Mildly annoyed, perhaps embarrassed by visible flakes
**What you can do:** Recommend zinc pyrithione or ketoconazole shampoos, suggest gentle scalp exfoliation

### Seborrhoeic Dermatitis

More significant than dandruff and often mistaken for it. Look for **red, inflamed patches** with **greasy, yellowish scales**. It tends to appear in areas with high sebum production — the hairline, behind the ears, at the crown.

**What it looks like:** Yellow-greasy scale on red, inflamed base
**How the client feels:** Itchy, self-conscious, frustrated that "nothing works"
**What you can do:** Suggest medicated shampoos (antifungal like ketoconazole), avoid heavy styling products on the scalp, recommend they see a pharmacist or GP if persistent

### Psoriasis

**Thick, well-defined plaques** covered with **dry, silvery-white scales**. Psoriasis plaques have sharp borders — you can often see exactly where normal scalp ends and the plaque begins. A key feature: psoriasis commonly extends **beyond the hairline onto the forehead or around the ears**.

**What it looks like:** Thick silvery plaques with sharp borders, often at hairline
**How the client feels:** Varies from mildly bothered to deeply distressed; some clients have had it for years
**What you can do:** Be sensitive in conversation, avoid aggressive brushing over plaques, suggest they see their GP for management options. Coal tar shampoos may help mild cases.

### Contact Dermatitis

A reaction to something that has touched the scalp — **hair dye, shampoo, styling products, or fragrance**. This is particularly relevant in the salon because **you may be the cause**. Contact dermatitis presents as redness, itching, and sometimes tiny blisters in the area where the product was applied.

**What it looks like:** Red, itchy, sometimes blistered — follows the pattern of product application
**How the client feels:** Uncomfortable, possibly alarmed
**What you can do:** Identify and remove the offending product, suggest patch testing before future chemical services, document the reaction

> Here's my rule: if it's red, raised, spreading, or painful — it needs more than a product change. That's when you guide the client towards professional help, calmly and confidently.

## Telling Them Apart

The key visual differences:

| Feature | Dandruff | Seb Derm | Psoriasis | Contact Derm |
|---------|----------|----------|-----------|--------------|
| **Scale** | White, dry | Yellow, greasy | Silvery, thick | None or fine |
| **Redness** | Minimal | Moderate | Marked | Moderate-marked |
| **Borders** | Diffuse | Diffuse | Sharp, well-defined | Follows product area |
| **Beyond hairline?** | No | Sometimes | Often | Follows application |

## Key Takeaways

- You don't need to diagnose — you need to recognise and guide
- Dandruff is dry and white; seb derm is greasy and yellow; psoriasis is thick and silvery
- Contact dermatitis follows the pattern of product application — consider whether salon products are the cause
- Any red, spreading, or painful condition needs professional assessment
- Your confident, calm guidance makes a huge difference to worried clients

## Reflection

Think about the last few clients where you noticed something on their scalp but didn't feel confident enough to say anything. With the knowledge from this lesson, what would you say to them now?

lessons.content:
## Normal vs Concerning

Clients mention hair loss to their stylist more than to any other professional. Sometimes it's a passing comment — "I've been shedding a bit more lately" — and sometimes it's a genuine cry for help. This lesson helps you distinguish between normal shedding and the signs that something needs attention.

## Understanding Normal Shedding

**Normal hair shedding is 50-100 hairs per day.** That sounds like a lot, but on a head with 80,000-120,000 hairs, it's less than 0.1% daily. These hairs have completed their natural growth cycle and are being replaced by new growth.

Clients often notice shed hair more at certain times:
- **During washing** — hair that was going to shed naturally is loosened
- **During brushing** — especially if they don't brush daily
- **Seasonal changes** — some people shed more in autumn, though the research is mixed

> When a client tells me they're "losing clumps of hair," my first question is always about context. Are they finding a few hairs on the pillow and panicking, or are they genuinely seeing thinning? Your calm perspective is incredibly valuable.

## When Shedding Becomes a Concern

### Telogen Effluvium (TE)

**What it is:** A temporary but significant increase in shedding, caused by a trigger that pushes a large number of follicles into the resting (telogen) phase simultaneously. The shedding typically begins **2-3 months after the trigger**.

**Common triggers:**
- Major illness, surgery, or high fever
- Significant emotional stress
- Crash dieting or rapid weight loss
- Postpartum (2-4 months after giving birth)
- Starting or stopping medications (including contraceptive pills)
- COVID-19 (increasingly common trigger)

**What you'll notice:** Diffuse thinning — the client's ponytail feels thinner, the part looks wider, they're finding more hair everywhere. The hairs themselves look normal — full length with a white club bulb at the root.

**The reassurance:** TE is almost always temporary. Once the trigger resolves, normal cycling resumes, and regrowth begins within 6-9 months. Your reassurance, backed by knowledge, is powerful.

### Pattern Hair Loss (Androgenetic Alopecia)

The most common form of progressive hair loss in both men and women.

**In men:** Typically begins with recession at the temples and thinning at the crown, eventually progressing to the classic horseshoe pattern of remaining hair.

**In women:** Usually presents as a **widening part line** and diffuse thinning across the crown, with preservation of the frontal hairline. Complete baldness is rare in women.

**What you'll notice:** Gradual thinning over months or years. The hair itself may feel finer in the thinning areas. Unlike TE, pattern hair loss doesn't involve dramatic shedding — it's a slow reduction in hair thickness and density.

### Traction Alopecia

This is the hair loss condition you can directly help prevent. **Traction alopecia** is caused by **sustained tension on the hair** from tight styling — ponytails, braids, cornrows, extensions, weaves, and even tight religious head coverings.

**What you'll notice:** Thinning or loss along the **tension lines** — typically at the hairline, temples, or above the ears. In early stages, you may see short broken hairs. In advanced stages, the hair may not regrow because the follicles have been permanently damaged.

**Your role:** This is where you make a direct difference. Educate clients about tension, suggest alternative styles, and be honest when you see the early signs.

### Alopecia Areata

**Smooth, round patches** of complete hair loss, usually appearing suddenly. The skin in the patches looks normal — no redness, no scale. This is an **autoimmune condition** and always needs referral to a specialist.

**What you'll notice:** One or more smooth, circular bare patches. The client may be distressed or may not have noticed the patch themselves (especially if it's at the back of the head).

## How to Respond

1. **Don't panic.** Your calm response sets the tone.
2. **Acknowledge.** "Thank you for mentioning this — it's good that you've noticed."
3. **Observe.** Note the pattern, distribution, and any changes to the scalp skin.
4. **Guide.** Depending on what you see, suggest appropriate next steps.
5. **Follow up.** Check in at their next appointment.

## Key Takeaways

- Normal shedding is 50-100 hairs per day — context matters more than count
- Telogen effluvium is temporary and resolves once the trigger passes
- Pattern hair loss is progressive but manageable — early conversation helps
- Traction alopecia is preventable — you are the first line of defence
- Smooth patches of complete loss (alopecia areata) always need referral

## Reflection

A long-time client who always wears very tight high ponytails mentions she's noticed her hairline receding. How would you start the conversation, and what would you suggest?

lessons.title: Starting the conversation
lessons.description: Safe, supportive language for sensitive topics
lessons.content:
## The Power of Your Words

Hair and scalp concerns are deeply personal. For many clients, their hair is tied to their identity, their confidence, and their sense of self. How you start a conversation about a concern can either open a door to trust or shut it completely.

This lesson gives you the language tools to raise sensitive topics with care, listen effectively, and guide clients towards the help they need — all within your professional boundaries.

## Opening the Door

The best conversations start with **observation, not opinion**.

### Safe Opening Phrases

- "I've noticed some changes here — have you noticed anything?"
- "Your scalp looks a little different from your last visit — has anything changed for you?"
- "I can see there's some sensitivity here — is this something that's been bothering you?"

### Phrases to Avoid

- "You're losing your hair" — too blunt, too alarming
- "You have [condition name]" — you're not diagnosing
- "You should see a doctor immediately" — creates panic
- "That doesn't look right" — vague and frightening

> The difference between a good conversation and a bad one often comes down to three words: "Have you noticed?" Those words give the client agency. They invite sharing rather than imposing a verdict.

## Active Listening

Once the client starts talking, your most important job is to **listen**. Active listening means:

- **Full attention** — put down tools, make eye contact, give them your focus
- **Reflection** — "It sounds like this has been really worrying for you"
- **Validation** — "I completely understand why you'd feel that way"
- **Clarification** — "Can you tell me a bit more about when you first noticed this?"
- **Patience** — let them finish before you respond. Silence is okay.

Don't jump to solutions immediately. A client who feels heard is more likely to follow your guidance than one who feels rushed.

## Framing Referrals Positively

When you need to suggest the client sees a specialist, frame it as a **positive step**, not an alarming one.

**Good framing:**
- "I think a trichologist could give you really clear answers on this — they specialise in exactly this kind of thing"
- "Your GP can run some simple tests that would help us understand what's going on"
- "There are specialists who deal with this every day — they'd be a great next step"

**Poor framing:**
- "I can't help you with this" — feels like rejection
- "You need to see a doctor" — sounds urgent and scary
- "This is beyond my expertise" — undermines client confidence in you

## Managing Emotional Responses

Some clients will become emotional. That's natural and appropriate. When it happens:

- **Acknowledge the emotion** — "I can see this is upsetting, and that's completely understandable"
- **Offer privacy** — move to a quieter area if possible
- **Don't minimise** — avoid "It's not that bad" or "Lots of people deal with this"
- **Be steady** — your calm presence is reassuring
- **Don't make promises** — "I'm sure it'll grow back" isn't helpful if you don't know

## Practicing the Conversation

Role-play is the best way to build confidence with sensitive conversations. Practice these scenarios with a colleague:

1. A client with visible thinning at the temples who hasn't mentioned it
2. A client who asks you directly if they're going bald
3. A client who becomes tearful when discussing their hair loss
4. A client who insists you "diagnose" what's wrong with their scalp

## Key Takeaways

- Lead with observation, not opinion: "I've noticed..." not "You have..."
- Active listening builds more trust than immediate solutions
- Frame referrals as positive steps, not alarming ones
- Acknowledge emotions without minimising them
- Practice sensitive conversations — confidence comes from rehearsal

## Reflection

Think about a conversation you found difficult or awkward with a client about their hair. With the language tools from this lesson, how would you handle it differently next time?
